title: Approximate planning over memoryless stochastic POMDP policies
short_statement: Find an exact or provably approximate algorithm for optimizing stochastic memoryless policies in finite POMDPs.
open_problem: Give a globally valid exact or approximation algorithm for finite POMDP planning restricted to stochastic memoryless policies.
background: POMDPs are a standard operations-research and AI model for sequential decision making under incomplete state observation. They model maintenance with hidden machine condition, medical treatment with latent patient state, robot navigation with noisy sensors, and inventory/control systems with partial information. Full POMDP planning is difficult because the belief state is continuous and optimal policies may require memory. Memoryless stochastic policies are a natural restricted class: they are compact, implementable, and often used in policy-gradient methods. The surprising difficulty is that even this restricted class is globally nonconvex. This makes the problem a clean theoretical target: the model is already well defined, the policy class is fixed, and the open question is whether there is a tractable exact or approximate global optimizer.
full_statement: Consider a finite discounted partially observable Markov decision process with state space $S$, action space $A$, observation space $O$, transition kernel $P(s'\mid s,a)$, observation kernel $Z(o\mid s',a)$, reward function $r(s,a)$, initial distribution $\rho$, and discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$. A stochastic memoryless policy is a matrix $\pi(a\mid o)$ that maps only the current observation to an action distribution; it does not keep a belief state or history. Its value is $$V(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\left[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)\right].$$ The policy class is finite-dimensional but nonconvex: the stationary occupancy measures and value are rational functions of the policy variables because the hidden state evolves under an observation-action feedback loop. The open problem, as posed in the COLT open-problem paper of Azizzadenesheli, Lazaric, and Anandkumar, is to design a method that finds an exact optimal stochastic memoryless policy or an approximate policy with a provable global guarantee for general finite POMDPs in this class. The problem is not to solve the full belief-state POMDP with arbitrary history-dependent policies; the benchmark is the best policy within the memoryless stochastic class.
known_results: Classical POMDP theory gives dynamic-programming structure for finite horizons and belief-state formulations for infinite horizons, but those algorithms optimize over history- or belief-dependent policies and scale poorly. Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis established fundamental computational hardness for Markov decision processes and imperfect-information control models. For memoryless stochastic POMDP policies specifically, Azizzadenesheli, Lazaric, and Anandkumar stated the COLT open problem: despite the small parametric policy class, finding an exact or approximate optimal stochastic memoryless policy remains open. Montufar, Ghazi-Zahedi, and Ay studied the geometry and determinism of optimal stationary control in POMDPs and showed structural facts such as limited stochasticity of optimal memoryless policies. Muller and Montufar later described the value and occupancy geometry as rational functions and polynomial constraints, giving a precise algebraic picture of the nonconvex feasible set. These results clarify the landscape, but they do not provide a polynomial-time approximation theorem or a global optimization method with worst-case guarantees.

progress.summary: The problem has a clean algebraic formulation and many local/policy-gradient heuristics, but no general exact or approximation guarantee for globally optimizing stochastic memoryless POMDP policies.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite POMDPs can expose local optima, integrality gaps in relaxations, or hardness gadgets. Candidate instances can be enumerated and optimized by exact polynomial/nonlinear programming for small sizes.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can generate small POMDPs with many poor local optima, test policy-gradient failures, and search for relaxations with large gaps. A full positive result still needs a proof over all finite POMDPs.

literature.synthesis: The open problem is narrow but deep. Classical POMDP algorithms work in belief space and do not solve the restricted parametric optimization problem efficiently. The COLT open-problem paper isolates memoryless policies because they are implementable and statistically natural in reinforcement learning, yet their objective is globally nonconvex. Later geometric work makes this nonconvexity explicit: the achievable occupancy measures satisfy polynomial constraints, and rewards are rational functions of policy probabilities. This suggests two possible routes: exploit algebraic structure for approximation, or prove hardness/no-approximation results for the restricted class. At present the literature gives structural insight and local methods, not a globally guaranteed planner.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Try polynomial-optimization relaxations with certified approximation ratios, exploit limited-stochasticity structure to reduce support patterns, or prove hardness through reductions that keep the observation-action policy matrix small. Computational work should search for minimal hard POMDP instances and compare exact global optima with policy-gradient and SDP/SoS relaxations.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A solution must optimize against the best stochastic memoryless policy, not the best deterministic memoryless policy unless a theorem shows deterministic suffices for the stated model. It must specify finite/infinite horizon, discount or average reward, initial distribution, and whether the transition and observation kernels are rationally encoded. Approximation guarantees should be global and worst-case, not local stationarity guarantees. For lower bounds, verify that the reduction preserves the memoryless-policy restriction and does not rely on history-dependent behavior.
